results.summary_before: AlphaOneSoC is a 32-bit RISC-V SoC based on Michael Bell's TinyQV, implementing the RV32EC ISA. It boots from external QSPI flash or PSRAM and provides UART, SPI, and GPIO interfaces for interaction and debugging. Testing involves flashing instructions into memory and observing outputs via UART, SPI, or GPIO. The design requires a QSPI flash/PSRAM PMOD and is a larger 3x2 tile submission.

results.summary_before: This is a toy neural network accelerator aimed at convolutional neural networks, containing 16-bit floating point add and multiply units using an approximation of the BF16 encoding. It supports a 4x2 convolution operation with streamed image pixels and an accumulate operation with optional bias and ReLU, all controlled by operation codes sent over a 16-bit input formed from ui_in and uio_in. Results are emitted as 16-bit values split over two clock cycles on the 8-bit output, so the user must know which cycles carry valid data. The Verilog is generated from a separate SystemVerilog repository that holds the full verification environment and software, both described as work in progress at tapeout time, and no specific external hardware is required beyond something to drive the sequences, such as the demo board's RP2040.

results.summary_before: This project recreates the classic Checkers demo from VGA Playground, with each of its five layers generated by a different Python-based HDL: Amaranth, MyHDL, PyCDE, PyRTL and PyMTL3. It outputs VGA signals on the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout at a 25.175 MHz clock, and the eight input pins can be toggled to change the main, sub, foreground and background colours. The only external hardware needed is the TinyVGA PMOD and a screen, and the design is notable for demonstrating several Python HDLs in a single chip. It is essentially a visual demonstration rather than a functional application.

results.summary_before: This is a digital saw-wave synthesizer with a programmable pulse generator, ADSR amplitude modulation, a one-pole IIR filter, and a first-order delta-sigma audio output. Parameters are set over an SPI slave interface, and a trigger input starts and stops notes; a VST/CLAP plugin generates the SPI commands. It is an educational design that deliberately mirrors the audio pipeline structurally in hardware, and it requires an external lowpass filter, button Pmod, audio Pmod, and SPI master. Testing uses a cocotb testbench that writes audio to a file and compares against a golden reference.

results.summary_before: This design drives a 7-segment display from a counter whose period is either fixed or pseudo-random, selected by an input pin. A second input chooses between a hexadecimal sequence and a fixed text string, and the low 8 bits of a 24-bit counter are exposed on the bidirectional pins. It is tested on the Tiny Tapeout evaluation board by observing the display and changing the two select inputs. The design is notable mainly as a simple display and LFSR demonstration.
